tasks.short: Explain and practise safe behaviour on walks and at home, correct unsafe behaviour, and tell parents what happened.

steps.what: Nanny explains road safety and dangers to the children on walks
Nanny practises crossing the street and asking an adult for help
Nanny stops children touching unsafe objects and explains why
Nanny writes the parents a message about the day's safety moments: free text in a chat today, in the day report after the change
Nanny reads the final message: the safety moments are described as they happened and it goes to this child's parents
Nanny sends the checked message to the parents

tasks.design: A day report in the agency's parent app ({OTHER}) has quick fields for the routine lines (walk taken, crossings practised) and a free field where the nanny still writes the notable moments; the nanny reads the report and sends it to the parents. Teaching safe behaviour stays fully with the nanny.
tasks.previous_blocker: Nothing blocked it; this is hands-on teaching.
tasks.enabler_now: Dutch parent apps hold a daily report parents can read.
tasks.still_hard: Safety is taught by example and repetition on the street.
tasks.human_edge: Holding a small hand at the kerb and making the lesson stick.

reach.task: Teach road safety on group outings
reach.learn: Whether day reports capture safety moments parents care about.

evidence.claim: A Dutch parent app gives parents a daily report in a digital diary.

assumptions: Boundary: from teaching on walks to telling parents; incidents needing medical care are outside.
Input contract: day report fields set by the agency; fallback is a chat message.

Teaching, practising and correcting keep their full time, and so do reading and sending the message. s4 keeps 85 because only the routine lines become quick fields; the safety moments are still written by the nanny.
Scenario: the nanny works through an agency with a parent app.
unknowns: Whether the family uses an agency app or a chat group.
research_questions: Do parents prefer structured day reports to free messages?

incremental.description: No ongoing upkeep: the agency sets the day report fields, and learning them is a one-off.

approvals.approved_version: The day message with the safety moments exactly as read by the nanny in s4c, sent once to this child's parents in the parent app; any change needs a new read.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: the parents keep the chat and the nanny types the message as today (0.0); high: the day report's quick fields cover the routine lines (0.4).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Check the home for hazards, secure them, agree rules with parents, post house rules and emergency numbers, and explain rules to the children.

steps.what: Nanny checks the house and garden for hazards each day
Nanny removes hazards or secures them with locks and gates
Nanny agrees house rules and boundaries with the parents
Parents enter emergency numbers and medical contacts in the family profile
Nanny writes the agreed house rules into the family profile, checks the numbers the parents entered and prints the sheet for the fridge
Nanny explains the rules to the children

tasks.design: A family profile template in the agency's parent app ({OTHER}) holds house rules, emergency numbers and medical contacts. The parents enter the numbers and contacts; the nanny writes the agreed rules, checks the numbers and prints the sheet for the fridge. Checking for hazards, securing them and explaining rules stay with the nanny.
tasks.previous_blocker: Rules and numbers lived on handwritten sheets that went out of date.
tasks.enabler_now: Parent apps hold family profiles and contact details.
tasks.still_hard: Spotting hazards is constant attention; the profile only helps if parents keep it current.
tasks.human_edge: Seeing the danger before the child does.

reach.task: Look after the children for an evening
reach.learn: Whether a shared family profile helps stand-ins.

evidence.claim: A Dutch parent app shows parents a timeline, daily report and agenda.
Medical contacts and health notes are special-category data; only the people who need them should see them.

assumptions: Boundary: from checking the home to children told the rules; home repairs are outside.
Input contract: family profile kept by the parents with the nanny; fallback is a handwritten sheet.
Parent time, including entering the numbers (s3p, share 1), is outside the nanny's savings.
Checking, securing, agreeing and explaining keep their full time. s4 keeps 70: the nanny no longer copies numbers from the parents but still writes the rules, checks the numbers and prints.
unknowns: Whether the agency app has a family profile.
research_questions: Do stand-in carers find rules and numbers faster?

incremental.description: Nanny updates the family profile when rules change.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: the parents do not fill in the profile, so the nanny types the numbers too and only the layout is saved (0.7); high: the parents enter numbers and contacts (2.5).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Help children eat, rest and use the toilet, teach the habits, and record meals, sleep and nappies for the parents.

steps.what: Nanny helps children with eating and teaches table habits
Nanny keeps resting routines and puts children down for naps
Nanny helps with toilet training and hygiene
Nanny writes meals, sleep and nappies in a paper notebook for the parents

tasks.design: Meals, sleep times and nappies are tapped into quick fields of the day report in the agency's parent app ({OTHER}) during the day instead of written up in a notebook. Helping children with eating, resting and toileting stays as it is. Recording meals, sleep and nappies belongs to the record-keeping task 39-9011.01:2366 and is priced there at its full time, because tapping fields instead of writing saves no time; helping the children does not change.
tasks.previous_blocker: The paper notebook was filled in at the end of the day from memory.
tasks.enabler_now: Dutch parent apps give parents a daily report in a digital diary.
tasks.still_hard: Health-related notes are special-category data and must be shared only with the parents.
tasks.human_edge: Patience at the table and on the potty.
tasks.altitude: Nothing changes; the log is always current for the parents.

reach.task: Log meals and sleep for a group of babies
reach.learn: Whether quick fields save as much time in a group.

evidence.claim: A Dutch parent app gives parents a daily report in a digital diary and asks for diary consent.
Health notes about a child are special-category data under the GDPR.

assumptions: Boundary: from meals to the day's log; medical care is outside.
Input contract: day report fields set by the agency; parents consent to the diary; fallback is the notebook.
Scenario: the nanny works through an agency with a parent app.
s4 is part of keeping meal records, which sibling task 39-9011.01:2366 covers; it is a first record and keeps its full time here and there.
unknowns: Whether the parents want a digital log.
research_questions: Do parents act sooner on eating or sleep changes with a live log?

incremental.description: No upkeep in this task; learning the quick fields is counted with sibling task 39-9011.01:2366.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: No saving in this task: the only changed step belongs to sibling task 39-9011.01:2366.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Think up age-appropriate activities, gather materials, do lap play, reading and crafts, and share what the child did.

steps.what: Nanny thinks up activities that fit the child's age and interests

loop.input: The child's age band, an interest the nanny names and the materials at home.
loop.output: Three ideas: a lap game, a book theme and a simple craft with steps.
loop.check: Ideas must fit the age band's safety list (no small parts under three, no hot tools); materials must be on the home list; no child name or personal data goes in; the nanny reads each idea before use.
loop.stop: One draft and one redraft; then the nanny picks from habit.
loop.why_not_simpler: Fresh ideas around a child's passing interest are creative work; a list of standard games goes stale.

steps.what: Nanny gathers or buys materials for the activity
Nanny does lap play, reading and arts and crafts with the child
Nanny writes a note on what the child did and picks photos for the parents: in a chat today, in the day report after the change
Nanny reads the final report: the note matches what the child did, the photos show only this child, and it goes to this child's parents
Nanny sends the checked report with photos to the parents

tasks.design: A bounded step drafts age-appropriate activity ideas from an interest the nanny names, checked against an age safety list and the home's materials, and the nanny chooses. The nanny writes the note and picks photos in the day report of the agency's parent app ({OTHER}), where date and activity type are fields; the nanny reads the report, checks that only this child is in the photos, and sends it; the activities themselves stay with the nanny and child.
tasks.previous_blocker: Ideas came from memory, and updates were chat messages typed at nap time.
tasks.enabler_now: Early-years tools draft activities from a child's interest, and parent apps hold photos and day reports.
tasks.still_hard: Drafts must be safe and fit the child; play itself is the job.
tasks.human_edge: Following the child's lead and turning a game into learning.

reach.learn: Whether the same draft step suits groups.

evidence.claim: An early-years tool drafts activity ideas from a child's interest; practitioners check them.
A Dutch parent app shows parents photos and a daily report, with photo consent asked at first login.
Parent-facing chatbots must say they are AI; this design has no chatbot.

assumptions: Boundary: from choosing activities to sharing them; schooling is outside.
Input contract: age safety list and home materials list kept by the nanny with the parents; no child data in the draft; fallback is ideas from memory.

Play, gathering materials, reading and sending the report keep their full time. s1 keeps 70 because the nanny still reads, judges and picks the ideas; only searching for them goes. s4 keeps 85 because the nanny still writes the note and picks photos; only the date and activity fields are filled.
Scenario: the nanny works through an agency with a parent app.
unknowns: Whether parents want photos through an app.
research_questions: Do drafted ideas widen the range of activities over a month?

already_counted.description: Nanny reads drafted ideas before use.

incremental.description: Nanny keeps the home materials list current.

approvals.approved_version: The note and the photos exactly as read by the nanny in s4c, sent once to this child's parents in the parent app; any change needs a new read.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: a nanny with a settled routine rarely asks for ideas and the parents keep the chat (0.7); high: ideas drafted for new activities and the day report used (4.6).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

role.altitude: The nanny keeps every moment of care, play and teaching; logs and messages move to quick fields in the parent app.
skills_to_grow: Keeping day reports short and useful
role.ambitious_version: A nanny whose day with the children is uninterrupted by paperwork.
